label: Keynesian mixed economy (post-war consensus)
description: A demand-led short run (consumption, investment, government, trade) on top of a slowly growing supply side (potential output). Prices respond to the output gap through an expectations-augmented Phillips curve.

mpc.note: Long-run marginal propensity to consume out of disposable income. Post-war estimates cluster around 0.7–0.9; 0.75 keeps the fiscal multiplier near 1.5, in line with the empirical range.

consumption_adjustment.note: Share of the gap between desired and actual consumption closed each quarter (habit and smoothing).

current_income_weight.note: Weight households put on this quarter's disposable income; the rest is expected long-run income along the economy's potential path (Friedman's permanent-income hypothesis). Stops a slump from feeding on itself indefinitely.

business_saving_share.note: Depreciation plus retained profits as a share of GDP: the wedge between GDP and household income. Roughly the 1949 gap between GDP ($272.5bn) and disposable income (about $188bn) after taxes and transfers.

investment_adjustment.note: Share of the gap between desired and actual fixed investment closed each quarter (planning and construction lags).

accelerator.note: How strongly desired investment responds to the output gap (capacity utilisation). A 1% gap raises desired investment by 1%. Together with consumption this gives a fiscal multiplier of roughly 1.5, in line with post-war estimates.

investment_rate_sensitivity.note: Desired investment falls about 3% for each point rise in the real interest rate.

long_expectations_weight.note: How far investors' long-horizon inflation expectations follow short-run expectations away from the anchor. Under the gold peg, long-run expectations stayed close to it, so a price spike does not collapse the real rate that investment responds to.

investment_corporate_tax_sensitivity.note: Desired investment falls about 5% for a 10-point rise in the corporate tax rate.

inventory_ratio.note: Desired inventories as a share of annual final sales (about two and a half months of sales).

inventory_adjustment.note: Share of an inventory surplus or shortfall corrected each quarter. Drives the short inventory recessions of 1949 and 1954.

public_capital_depreciation.note: Annual wear on public capital (roads, research base, schools).

public_capital_elasticity.note: Doubling the public capital stock raises potential output by about 4%. Low end of the Aschauer-style literature.

natural_unemployment.note: Unemployment rate consistent with a zero output gap in the early 1950s.

minimum_unemployment.note: Frictional floor: people between jobs. The post-war US low was about 2.5% in 1953.

okun_coefficient.note: Okun's law: each 1% of negative output gap adds about half a point of unemployment.

unemployment_adjustment.note: Share of the gap to Okun's-law unemployment closed each quarter (hiring and firing lags).

phillips_slope.note: Each 1% of output gap adds 0.35 points to annualised inflation.

expectations_persistence.note: Weight on last quarter's inflation in expected inflation; the rest is the anchor. The gold peg kept expectations fairly well anchored.

inflation_anchor.note: Long-run inflation expectation under the Bretton Woods gold peg.

overheating_threshold.note: Output gap (%) beyond which capacity bottlenecks make inflation accelerate sharply.

overheating_slope.note: Extra inflation per point of output gap beyond the overheating threshold.

capacity_ceiling.note: Output cannot exceed potential by more than this (%). Demand beyond it becomes shortages and inflation.

budget_phase_in.note: Share of a budget change that takes effect each quarter (appropriation and spending lags).

world_demand_growth.note: Real growth of foreign demand for exports during the post-war recovery.

import_tariff_elasticity.note: Responsiveness of import volumes to the tariff-inclusive import price.

import_propensity_trend.note: Yearly rise in the share of spending that goes on imports as Europe and Japan rebuild and trade integrates. With exports growing at world-demand pace, both trade shares climb together, as they did until about 1970.

neutral_real_rate.note: Real short-term interest rate consistent with a closed output gap and target inflation.

policy_inflation_response.note: How far the central bank's desired rate moves for each point of inflation above the anchor.

policy_gap_response.note: How far the central bank's desired rate moves for each point of output gap.

policy_rate_smoothing.note: Share of the gap to the desired rate closed each quarter; central banks move gradually.

policy_rate_max_step.note: Most the short rate moves in one quarter, in points. The Fed of the 1950s and 1960s moved the discount rate in quarter- and half-point steps and rarely more than a point in a quarter; until the Accord this never binds upwards because the peg caps the rate at 1.25%.

policy_rate_floor.note: Lowest short-term rate the central bank will set.

profit_cyclicality.note: Corporate profits swing about three times as much as output over the cycle.

income_tax_progressivity.note: Unindexed brackets: income-tax receipts rise faster than nominal income per head (bracket creep), an automatic stabiliser.

gold_settlement_share.note: Share of the overall balance of payments settled in gold; the rest accumulates as foreign-held dollars (the Triffin problem).

debt_rate_adjustment.note: Share of the debt stock refinanced at current long rates each quarter.

term_premium.note: Long-term yields over the bill rate once the Fed is free to set rates. Long Treasuries yielded roughly 0.8–1.5 points over bills in the early and mid-1950s. Under the peg the long rate stays pegged at its 1949 level.

long_rate_adjustment.note: Share of the gap between the long rate and the bill rate plus the term premium closed each quarter after the peg ends. Long yields drifted up from about 2.5% (1951) to about 3% (1953).

price_control_passthrough.note: Share of price rises above the anchor that still shows under a general freeze, whether from demand pressure (output gap, bottlenecks, shortages) or from expected inflation (wages are frozen too). The 1951 freeze took consumer-price inflation from about 8% (1951) to under 2% (1952) while demand stayed strong; something over a third leaked through reclassification, quality cuts and uncontrolled goods. Held-back demand pressure is stored and released later; held-back expectations are not.

price_control_leak.note: Share of the held-back price rises that leaks into prices each quarter while controls last (grey markets, exemptions, approved increases).

price_control_release.note: Share of the held-back price rises released each quarter after controls end. Prices rose in the year after the 1946 decontrol by about as much as had been suppressed; the 1953 decontrol released little because demand had cooled.

capital_share.note: Capital's share of income in the aggregate production function (Cobb–Douglas). The standard post-war estimate is about 0.3.

tfp_growth.note: Yearly growth of total factor productivity: output gained from better technique and organisation, beyond more capital and workers. US private-business estimates for 1948–73 run near 1.5–2%.

labour_force_growth.note: Yearly growth of the labour force in the 1950s. A placeholder until pops and demography drive it in Phase 3.

sector_capacity_ceiling.note: How far (%) one industry can run above its normal capacity with overtime and extra shifts. Industries stretch further than the economy as a whole, which is limited by labour.

investment_allocation_sensitivity.note: How strongly new investment flows to industries running hot. An industry 10% busier than average attracts 40% more of its usual share.

utilisation_smoothing.note: Weight on the latest quarter when investors judge how busy an industry is; the rest is its recent history.

surge_import_share.note: Share of an industry's shortage met by extra imports from abroad.

surge_import_cap.note: Extra imports can cover at most this share of a product's normal home use in one quarter.

ration_weight_consumption.note: How readily household purchases are cut when goods are short. Higher numbers are cut first.

ration_weight_investment.note: How readily business investment projects are delayed when goods are short.

ration_weight_inventories.note: How readily stockbuilding is abandoned when goods are short; firms give it up first.

ration_weight_government.note: How readily government orders are cut when goods are short. Low because defence contracts carry priority ratings (as under the Defense Production Act of 1950).

ration_weight_exports.note: How readily export orders are cut when goods are short.
